newsitem.title: USA: Election won, Clinton turns to reshaping cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Election won, Clinton turns to reshaping cabinet.

text.p: Newly re-elected, President Bill Clinton's first order of business will be to take a hard look at his Cabinet and White House staff and decide who stays and who goes.
As he learned in 1992, it is not an easy process.

"When you look at what we did at the end of 1992, it is obvious that mistakes were made. We didn't have a clue about what we were doing. We didn't even know what we didn't know," said one White House official.
"This is our last, best chance to get it right," he added.

Four years ago Clinton made some disastrous appointments, naming lawyer Zoe Baird attorney general only to withdraw her nomination as the nation's top law enforcement officer because she had not paid Social Security taxes for her nanny.
Intent on avoiding the mistakes of the past, Clinton has already put in place a system to fill the spots that are expected to open up as people leave or are given the boot.
On the outside, Vernon Jordan, a longtime Washington powerbroker, and former White House deputy chief of staff Erskine Bowles have been tapped to lead the transition.
On the inside, Chief of Staff Leon Panetta has taken the lead on how to reshuffle the Cabinet while Evelyn Lieberman, one of his deputies, was studying the key White House jobs.
Panetta said on Tuesday that no decisions had been made, but the new team might include some Republicans.
"It is going to be based hopefully on those who are best qualified to serve in those positions, and that could include some Republicans," Panetta told the NBC television network.
Here is a look at how some of the main jobs may change.
Chief of Staff
Panetta's first job may be to replace himself in the most powerful position in the White House next to the president.
Speaking on election night, Panetta made no secret of his plans to return to California, where he may run for governor.
"I'm going to continue to be chief of staff as we work through the transition," Panetta told ABC televison. "There's no secret that at some point I'll go back to California."

Clinton learned the sensitivity of the job the hard way, replacing his first chief of staff, childhood friend Thomas "Mack" McClarty, with Panetta after 18 months when the native Arkansan's lack of Washington expertise became a liability.

Many names have circulated to replace Panetta, including Deputy Chief of Staff Harold Ickes, Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor, and Bowles. Cited as dark horses are White House Counsel Jack Quinn, former New York Congressman Tom Downey and Lieberman.
Secretary of State
Secretary of State Warren Christopher, 71, is believed to want to retire after flying more than 700,000 miles (1.1 million km) on government business in the last four years.

But officials have said rumours of his imminent departure may be exaggerated, saying he is likely to stay on at least through the end of the year. One official suggested he could stay longer, depending on the Middle East peace talks.
His job, the most prestigious in the Cabinet, is also among the most sought after.
Potential successors include former Sen. George Mitchell, former Assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke and U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright.
Others include Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, Kantor and, as a long shot, retiring Georgia Sen. Sam Nunn.
Secetary of Defence
Defence Secretary William Perry, 69, has said he will not decide on retiring until after the election, but speaking two weeks ago he did not sound desperate to hang on to his job.
"It was not something I sought, something I was anxious to do," he told reporters. "It was something which was urged on me and after a lot of consideration I finally decided to do."
John Deutch, the director of the Central Intelligence Agency, is widely expected to move to Defence if Perry goes.
Secretary of the Treasury

Several White House officials said Rubin is expected to keep his job, saying he enjoys the position, seems perfectly suited to it and enjoys unrivaled access to the White House, where he attends the daily senior staff meeting at 7:30 a.m.
Attorney General

At the Justice Department, Janet Reno is seen as one of the more vulnerable members of the Cabinet. A month ago, Reno suggested she would like to be re-appointed, telling reporters she would "be honoured and ... would look forward to it."
But several White House officials said she may well be elbowed aside, for example if Kantor were to want her job.
